passage: By Friday the pantry on the third floor of the women's hostel had a sink full of sticky pans and a smell nobody wanted to name. Uma, twenty, stood in the doorway with her one mug. She had left a plate there on Monday, meaning to wash it later. So, it seemed, had everyone. Jaya came in behind her. "Whose is all this?" "Everyone's," said Uma. "And no one's." Jaya laughed without much humour. "I left a bowl. I thought one bowl didn't matter." "I thought one plate didn't matter." They looked at the tower of dishes, every piece of it somebody's "just one." Uma rolled up her sleeves. "Let's at least do ours." Jaya picked up a sponge, then hesitated. "And the rest?"

qa.q: On which floor was the pantry?
qa.a: The third floor of the women's hostel.

qa.q: How did Uma feel when she left her plate on Monday?
qa.a: She wasn't worried, meaning to wash it later and assuming one plate didn't matter.

qa.q: What choice do Uma and Jaya face at the end, and what might help beyond that night?
qa.a: Whether to wash only their own dishes or the rest too; a shared rota for the pantry could stop the pile from coming back.

qa.q: How might other hostel residents feel walking into the pantry on Friday?
qa.a: They may feel disgusted and annoyed, while quietly knowing that one of the dishes is theirs.

grounding: Hostel residents each leave one dish in a shared pantry, sure their bit is too small to matter, until the mess spoils it for everyone.

passage:
Subject: Our flat's kitchen, a confession

Hi Rajni,

You asked how flat life in Pune is going. The honest answer: our kitchen is a disaster, and I'm part of why. There are four of us. Each of us leaves just a cup or a pan, sure somebody else will deal with it, or that one pan is too small to count. Last week I found an ant trail from the sink to the sugar tin, and I wanted to blame the others. Then I counted: two of the dirty pans were mine. Nobody cooks there now because it's too gross, so we all spend money on takeaway. Funny, isn't it? Each of us saved five minutes, and together we lost the whole kitchen. I'm proposing a washing rota at our flat meeting on Sunday. Wish me luck.

Love,
Jasleen

qa.q: How many of the dirty pans were Jasleen's?
qa.a: Two of the dirty pans.

qa.q: How did Jasleen feel on finding the ant trail, and what changed that?
qa.a: Jasleen felt annoyed and wanted to blame the others, but counting the pans showed two were Jasleen's own.

qa.q: What is Jasleen proposing on Sunday, and why could it work?
qa.a: A washing rota, which makes each person's share visible so no one can assume someone else will clean.

qa.q: How might the other flatmates react to the proposal?
qa.a: They may feel defensive at first, but since nobody can cook in the kitchen now, they may welcome a fair rota.

grounding: A student admits that each flatmate, including themselves, leaves small messes assuming someone else will clean, until the shared kitchen is unusable.

passage: "Jahnavi, you'll laugh, but I learned economics from a frying pan." Akash grinned, though he sounded a little embarrassed. "Five of us in the PG shared one kitchen. First week, spotless. Then someone left a pan. Then I left a pan, because honestly, one more? Who'd notice? By week three there wasn't a clean pan in the house, and we were frying eggs in the lid of a pressure cooker. Every one of us thought we'd only added a tiny bit. The landlady threatened to lock the kitchen. What finally worked? A chart on the fridge with our names and days, and a rule: the kitchen gets locked for whoever skips twice. It took ten minutes to set up. We should have done it in week one."

qa.a: The lid of a pressure cooker.

qa.q: What finally worked, and why?
qa.a: A chart on the fridge with names and days, plus a rule locking the kitchen for anyone who skips twice, which made each share clear and enforced.

qa.q: How might the landlady have seen the kitchen by week three?
qa.a: The landlady likely saw a mess nobody owned, and threatened to lock the kitchen because no one was taking care of it.

passage: I'm Tenzin, and I share a co-living flat in Hyderabad with three others. This is what I saw this week, and I was part of it. On Monday Nirmala left the pressure cooker in the sink. On Tuesday Arvind left rice in a pan on the stove. I left my tiffin boxes on the counter, because honestly, what are two boxes? By Thursday the sink was blocked and the fridge smelled of old milk. Nobody said anything; we just ate out. Saturday was Nirmala's birthday. She had planned to cook biryani for all of us. She opened the kitchen door, stood there a long time, and closed it again. I can't say what she was thinking. She ordered food instead. I washed my two boxes that night, though it hardly touched the pile.

qa.q: What had Nirmala planned to cook on her birthday?
qa.a: She had planned to cook biryani for all of them.

qa.q: What did Tenzin believe about the tiffin boxes left on the counter?
qa.a: Tenzin believed two boxes were too small to matter, thinking 'what are two boxes?' when the others were leaving things too.

qa.q: What could the flatmates have done at the point where the sink was blocked and nobody spoke up?
qa.a: Someone could have called a short flat meeting and agreed who cleans on which day, instead of everyone eating out and waiting.

qa.q: How is Nirmala affected by the state of the kitchen on her birthday?
qa.a: She loses the birthday meal she planned to cook for everyone, and standing silently at the door suggests she is disappointed, though Tenzin cannot be sure what she thought.

grounding: Flatmates, including the narrator, each leave a little mess in the shared kitchen thinking it cannot matter, and the kitchen becomes unusable for everyone.

passage:
Week one. The student house in Melbourne had four rooms and one kitchen. Sahil, twenty, cooked dal on Monday and left the pot soaking. "I'll do it tomorrow," he told Dolma. She laughed. "My plate's in there too."

Week two. The pot was still there, under three frying pans, a tower of bowls and a colander nobody would own. Fruit flies hovered over the bin. Everyone ate toast in their rooms. Sahil walked past the sink each night thinking, one pot is nothing compared with all that.

Week three. Dolma pinned a list to the fridge: every dirty item and whose it was. Sahil read it slowly. The pot, two mugs, a pan, a fork. Each line was small. Together, his lines were a quarter of the mess.

qa.q: What did Dolma pin to the fridge in week three?
qa.a: She pinned a list of every dirty item and whose it was.

qa.q: What did Sahil think each night as he walked past the sink in week two?
qa.a: He felt unconcerned, thinking his one pot was nothing compared with all the other mess, so it did not seem to matter.

qa.q: What choice could Sahil make after reading Dolma's list?
qa.a: He could wash all his items that night and suggest the house agree on who cleans when, since the list shows his small bits added up to a quarter of the mess.

qa.q: How might the list look to the other housemates when they read it?
qa.a: Each of them might be surprised, like Sahil, to see their own small items adding up, and might feel embarrassed to find their name on so many lines.

grounding: In a shared student kitchen each housemate leaves a little mess assuming it is too small to matter, until the pile makes the kitchen unusable for everyone.

passage:
Week one: Baljeet, twenty, moved into a four-person flat in Chandigarh. By Thursday there were three greasy pans in the sink. Baljeet added a plate. Someone else will do them, Baljeet thought.
Week three: The sink was full, the counter sticky. Neelam, the flatmate from Shimla, came home, sighed, and ordered takeaway instead of cooking. Baljeet did the same. One more plastic box went into the overflowing bin.
Week five: A cockroach crawled out of the stack. Everyone stood in the kitchen, arms crossed. "It's not all mine," said one. "I only left one mug," said another. Baljeet realised every one of them had believed their own bit hardly counted. Neelam said quietly, "So all of us made this." They finally cleaned together, four people and a lot of soap, till midnight.

qa.a: A cockroach crawled out of the stack.

qa.q: What was Baljeet thinking when adding a plate in week one?

grounding: Flatmates each leave a little mess in a shared kitchen, assuming someone else will clean, until the mess grows and everyone suffers.

passage: Sarika, you're complaining about your flat's kitchen? Let me tell you about the Room 12 kitchen in our boys' hostel at the engineering college, 1996. I'm Saurabh, and there were eight of us sharing one small stove. Everyone cooked instant noodles at midnight and left the pan. I did too. I thought: one pan, what's one pan? By the end of term, the pans had grown fungus. Somebody's milk had turned to cheese in a cupboard. Rats moved in. We stopped cooking and spent all our pocket money on the canteen. Every single one of us blamed the others. Nobody thought it was his own pan that had started it. Finally the warden locked the kitchen for a month. Only then did we sit together, eight fools, and agree who cleaned which day.

qa.q: How many students shared the Room 12 kitchen?
qa.a: There were eight of us sharing one small stove.

qa.q: What was Saurabh thinking when leaving his pan?
qa.a: Saurabh thought one pan didn't matter, feeling careless and sure his share was too small to count.

qa.q: Why was sitting together to agree on cleaning days a turning point in the story?
qa.a: It ended the blame game by making each person responsible for a set day, so the kitchen could be used again.

qa.q: How might the warden have felt about locking the kitchen?
qa.a: The warden was probably fed up and frustrated, seeing that the students would not fix the mess themselves.

grounding: An elder recalls a hostel kitchen where each person left a little mess, assuming others would clean, until everyone suffered.

passage: The PG's water tank had run dry again, and there were only two buckets for the whole floor until evening. Sudha, twenty-one, looked into the shared kitchen: every vessel was dirty, a pot of dal was growing a skin, and someone's tea strainer had turned black. She had added her own plate on Monday; she'd been sure someone would wash up. So, it seemed, had Dhruv and the three others. Now there wasn't even water to cook rice. Dhruv came in, saw the mess, and groaned. "Who left all this?" Sudha opened her mouth to say "not me," then stopped. Her plate was on top. So was his mug. "All of us," she said. With the little water they had, they washed just enough to cook one meal together. The rest had to wait for the tanker.

qa.q: How many buckets were there for the whole floor?
qa.a: There were only two buckets for the whole floor.

qa.q: What was Sudha feeling when she stopped herself from saying "not me"?
qa.a: Sudha felt uncomfortable and guilty, seeing her own plate on top of the pile.

qa.q: What could the PG's residents do once the water returns?
qa.a: They could agree a daily washing rota or each wash their own vessels at once, so no one assumes someone else will.

qa.q: How might Dhruv feel when Sudha said "All of us"?
qa.a: Dhruv might feel caught out and a little embarrassed, recognising that his mug was part of it too.

grounding: Flatmates each leave a little mess in a shared kitchen, assuming someone else will clean, until everyone suffers, made worse by a water shortage.

passage:
Last year I shared a flat in Hyderabad with Lalit and two others. I'm Kunal, and I'll admit I was the worst kind of flatmate: the one who thinks he's not the problem.
Our kitchen had one rule, "clean as you go," which nobody followed. I would leave a greasy kadhai overnight, telling myself Lalit was messier. Lalit, I found out later, told himself the same about me.
By exam week, we were ordering food every night because no one could face the stove. We spent more, ate worse, and snapped at each other over small things.
Looking back, what strikes me is how reasonable each small choice felt. One kadhai. One night.

qa.q: What was the kitchen's one rule?
qa.a: Their rule was "clean as you go."

qa.q: How does Kunal seem to feel looking back on the greasy kadhai?
qa.a: Kunal feels a mix of regret and embarrassment, seeing that each small, reasonable-seeming choice added up to a kitchen nobody could use.

qa.q: What could the flatmates have done instead of a rule nobody followed?
qa.a: They could have set a simple turn for washing up, with each person's name, so no one could assume someone else would do it.

qa.q: How does Lalit seem to have seen the mess?
qa.a: Lalit told himself Kunal was messier, so he also felt his own part was too small to matter.

grounding: Illustrates a flatmate recalling how each person's small, reasonable-seeming mess in a shared kitchen added up to a problem everyone suffered from.

passage:
Warden's note, Block C pantry, second week of term.
The shared pantry on the second floor has become a problem. I inspected it on Monday: a stack of unwashed pans, curry dried on the stove and a smell that reached the corridor. When I asked the residents, each said the same: 'Not mine. I only left one plate.' Ujjwal admitted he hadn't washed his tea pan for three days because 'nobody else washes theirs'. Ramesh said he'd stopped cooking because the kitchen was too dirty to use. So now eight students are ordering food they can barely afford, and everyone is irritated with everyone. Next step: I will meet all eight residents on Thursday to agree a cleaning rota, with names on the door.

qa.a: Because nobody else washes theirs.

qa.q: How did Ujjwal seem to feel about his own unwashed pan?
qa.a: Ujjwal seemed unconcerned, even resentful, feeling his one pan didn't matter when nobody else washed theirs.

qa.q: Why is a rota with names on the door a good step?

qa.q: How is Ramesh affected by the dirty pantry?

passage:
Sunday night.
Our flat's kitchen is officially a crime scene. Four of us, one sink, and it's been piling up for a week. Tonight I wanted to make instant noodles and there was no clean pot. I stood there feeling righteous: I only left a cup and one spoon! Then I saw Naveen's pan, Kunal's plates and the rice pot nobody has touched since Wednesday. And I realised every one of us thinks 'my cup is small, it doesn't matter.' That's how you get a sink full of four people's 'small' things. Naveen walked in, saw me glaring at his pan, and said, 'Bro, your cup is in there too.' Fair. We ended up washing everything together at midnight, arguing about whose turn it was. Tomorrow I'm drawing up a rota.
Mridul

qa.a: A cup and one spoon.

qa.q: How did Mridul feel standing at the sink at first?
qa.a: Mridul felt righteous and annoyed, sure the small cup didn't count.

qa.q: What will a rota change in the flat?
qa.a: It will make each person's turn clear, so the 'small' things don't pile up waiting for someone else.

qa.a: Naveen points out calmly that Mridul's cup is in there too, which cuts through the blame.
